title: Testing and code quality
blurb: Unit vs integration, test doubles, what makes a test brittle, and how to answer 'what's your testing strategy' without bluffing.

questions.q: What makes a function easy to test?
choices: It is short, ideally under ten lines, so one test covers the whole body
It is pure: the same input gives the same output, with no side effects
It lives in its own file, so the test can import it and nothing else
It takes no parameters, so there are no input combinations left to test
questions.why: No setup, no mocks, no cleanup: call it and assert. That is why 'separate deciding from doing' is a testability strategy, not just style. A short function that reads the clock or the database still needs all of that setup.
questions.asked: An opener that leads into how you structure code so the logic can be tested without infrastructure.

questions.q: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
choices: A unit test is written by developers; an integration test is written by the QA team
A unit test checks one piece alone; an integration test checks pieces working together
A unit test runs in CI on every push; an integration test runs on a developer's machine
A unit test calls a function directly; an integration test always drives the UI
questions.why: The boundary is a judgement call; a test hitting a real database is integration by most definitions. What matters is what each catches: unit tests catch logic errors, integration tests catch wiring errors. Driving the UI is an end-to-end test.
questions.asked: A definition every interviewer checks before asking about your own testing strategy.

questions.q: What is the usual criticism of the testing pyramid (many unit, fewer integration, few end-to-end tests)?
choices: It puts end-to-end tests at the base, which makes the whole suite slow, flaky and costly to run
It only applies to backend services, so frontends get no guidance from it
Mocked unit tests can all pass while the wiring between units, where bugs ship, is broken
It forbids integration tests, so database bugs are only found in production
questions.why: The 'testing trophy' argument: most real defects live in the wiring between units, so a suite of heavily mocked unit tests can be green while the app is broken. Either shape is defensible if you can explain what it buys.
questions.asked: 'What's your testing strategy?': this is where a considered opinion beats a diagram.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
choices: A stub is generated by a library, while a mock is always written by hand for the test
A mock replaces a whole database, while a stub replaces only a single function
A stub is used only in unit tests, while a mock is used only in integration tests
A stub returns canned values; a mock also verifies it was called in an expected way
questions.why: Mocks couple the test to how the code works. Asserting 'saveUser was called once with X' breaks on a legitimate refactor; asserting on the resulting state does not. Both can be hand-written or generated, at any test level.
questions.asked: The follow-up is when you would prefer asserting state over verifying calls.

questions.q: What makes a test brittle?
choices: It asserts on implementation details rather than on observable behaviour
It reads real data from a fixture file instead of values built inside the test
It runs for several seconds, so developers skip it when testing locally
It has more than one assertion, so one small change fails several checks
questions.why: Whole-DOM snapshots, mocks asserting internal call order, tests reaching into private state: they fail on every refactor and stop being trusted. A slow test is a cost, not brittleness, and several assertions about one behaviour are fine.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can explain why a suite gets deleted or ignored, which is the real cost of brittleness.

questions.q: A test passes locally and fails in CI intermittently. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A CI configuration error, since a real bug would fail on every single run
Shared state, order dependence, timing, or time zone and locale assumptions
The test is too slow and CI kills it, which is reported as an assertion failure
A dependency missing from CI that your machine has installed globally
questions.why: Intermittent failures come from tests that depend on each other, on wall-clock timing, on real network calls or on the machine's locale. A missing dependency would fail every run. A flaky test is worse than none: it teaches people to re-run until green.
questions.asked: A scenario question everyone with real experience has an answer to.

questions.q: What does test coverage actually tell you?
choices: How well the code is tested, since every covered line has been verified correct
Roughly how many bugs remain, because uncovered lines are where defects hide
Which lines ran during the tests, not whether the assertions checked anything
Whether every branch is correct, since branch coverage checks each outcome
questions.why: You can reach 100% with tests that assert nothing. Coverage is useful as a floor that points at untested files, and harmful as a target people game. Branch coverage only says both paths ran.
questions.asked: Checks whether you would push back on a coverage target used as a quality metric.

questions.q: What is TDD, in one sentence?
choices: Write the tests after the code, but before the pull request is opened for review
Write a test for every function, including private helpers, before shipping
Design the full test suite up front, then build features until it all passes
Write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest change, then refactor
questions.why: Red, green, refactor, in small steps. The value is design pressure (you must decide the shape of the code before writing it) and proof that each test can fail. Designing the whole suite up front is the opposite of the small-step loop.
questions.asked: A definition check; the follow-up is whether you actually practise it and when you do not.

questions.q: Why write the failing test first, rather than writing the test after the fix?
choices: A test that has never failed has not been shown to detect the bug it targets
It is faster, because the fix is then written with the test already in place
It raises coverage more than writing the same test after the fix would
Most CI systems reject a fix commit that does not first add a failing test
questions.why: Plenty of tests pass because they assert the wrong thing. Watching it go red and then green proves the link between the test and the behaviour. The same test written afterwards gives identical coverage.
questions.asked: Separates people who have seen a test pass for the wrong reason from people who have not.

questions.q: Should a unit test hit the real database?
choices: Yes; every test should use the real database, since mocks can never be trusted
No; no test at any level should touch a database, only mocked repositories
Only in CI, where a real database exists; locally the very same tests should use a mock instead
No, but integration tests should, because in-memory fakes hide real SQL and constraints
questions.why: EF Core's in-memory provider neither enforces constraints nor translates SQL, so tests can pass against behaviour the real database rejects. A real database in a container (Testcontainers) in the pipeline is the modern answer.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what in-memory fakes silently skip.

questions.q: What should a good test name communicate?
choices: The name of the function under test, so the test file mirrors the source file
The scenario and the expected outcome, so a failure is clear from the name alone
The ticket number, so the requirement behind the test can be looked up later
The author and the date, so questions about the test go to the right person
questions.why: `rejects_transfer_when_balance_is_insufficient` tells you what broke from the CI summary; `test_transfer_2` means opening the file. A function name alone does not say which behaviour failed.
questions.asked: Interviewers read your tests; names are the first thing they see.

questions.q: What is arrange-act-assert?
choices: A naming convention where each test name lists its arrange, act and assert steps
A structure: set up the state, perform one action, then assert on the result
A mocking style in which every dependency is arranged as a mock before acting
An order for CI stages: prepare the environment, deploy, then run smoke tests
questions.why: One action per test. A test that acts three times and asserts after each is really three tests, and its failure message will not tell you which part broke.
questions.asked: A structure check; strong candidates add "one behaviour per test".

questions.q: What is a property-based test?
choices: Checking that an object's properties have the right types after construction
Asserting an invariant that must hold for many generated inputs, not hand-picked ones
Testing configuration properties, such as each environment's settings file
Generating ordinary example-based tests automatically from each function's type signature
questions.why: 'Reversing a list twice gives the original' or 'the parser round-trips everything the serialiser produces'. The library generates and shrinks inputs, so it finds edge cases you would never have written by hand.
questions.asked: A depth signal; mentioning shrinking to a minimal failing case shows real use.

questions.q: How do you test code that depends on the current time?
choices: Run the test at a fixed time of day in CI, so the clock is always predictable
Use a very short timeout so the time barely changes while the test runs
Make the current time an input, via an injected clock or fake timers, fixed in the test
Compare dates with a tolerance of one whole day, so any time of day gives the same test result
questions.why: Treat the ambient clock like any other dependency and control it. An injected clock (.NET 8's `TimeProvider`) and fake timers (`mock.timers` in node:test, `jest.useFakeTimers`) are both implementations of that idea. Scheduling CI at a set hour still breaks on the developer's machine and around daylight saving.
questions.asked: Checks whether you design for testability; tests that fail at midnight are the follow-up.

questions.q: A non-urgent bug is reported in production. Once you understand it, what is the best first step?
choices: Fix it and deploy straight away, then add a test in a follow-up ticket
Add logging around the code and wait for it to happen again to confirm it
Write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it so the test goes green
Fix it and add a step to the manual QA checklist so each release checks it
questions.why: A regression test is the easiest test to justify: it catches a real bug, because it just did. For an outage the order changes: restore service first by rolling back or mitigating, then write this test as part of the fix.
questions.asked: 'Walk me through how you fix a production bug': the test belongs in the answer, after service is restored if it was an outage.

questions.q: What is the risk of mocking a third-party client heavily?
choices: Mocks run slower than the real client, because every call goes through a proxy
Mocking a library's classes breaches its licence unless you pay for a plan
The mock must be regenerated on every library upgrade, or the build fails to compile at all
Your mock encodes your assumptions, so tests pass even if the real API behaves otherwise
questions.why: The mock agrees with you by construction. Contract tests or a recorded-response fake keep you honest; at minimum, run one integration test against the real service somewhere.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know where mocks stop protecting you.

questions.q: What does code review add that tests do not?
choices: Faster feedback, since a reviewer usually replies before the pipeline has even finished
Judgement on design, naming, missing cases and whether the change should exist
A coverage check, since reviewers confirm each changed line has a test
Formatting consistency, since reviewers catch style that a linter cannot
questions.why: Tests verify the code does what it does. Review asks whether that is the right thing, whether someone will understand it in six months, and whether a case is missing entirely. Style belongs to the formatter.
questions.asked: Checks what you think review is for; nitpicking style is the answer that worries interviewers.

questions.q: What makes a pull request easy to review?
choices: Bundling every related refactor in, so the whole change needs only one review
Splitting it into one PR per file, so each reviewer only reads one file
Keeping tests out of it, so the diff is short and reviewers focus on the code
Small, one concern, a clear what-and-why description, and no unrelated churn
questions.why: Review quality drops sharply with size: a 1,000-line PR gets 'LGTM'. Keep the refactor in a separate commit or PR from the behaviour change so the reviewer can see what actually changed. Splitting by file cuts one concern into pieces nobody can judge alone.
questions.asked: A team-fit question as much as a technical one.

questions.q: When is it reasonable not to write a test?
choices: For a throwaway spike, or trivial code where a test would only restate the implementation
When the deadline is tight, as long as a ticket to add the missing tests goes into the backlog
For UI code, since interface behaviour cannot be tested automatically
When coverage is already above the team's threshold for that module
questions.why: A test asserting that a getter returns its field costs maintenance and catches nothing. Being able to say where tests do not pay is more credible than 'test everything'. UI behaviour is very testable, and 'later' tickets rarely get done.
questions.asked: Tests pragmatism; "never skip tests" and "skip when busy" are both weak answers.

questions.q: What is a smoke test in a deployment pipeline?
choices: The full regression suite, re-run against production after every single deploy
A short load test that checks the new version can handle peak traffic
A security scan of the deployed app for known vulnerable endpoints
A minimal check after deploy that the app is up and its critical path works
questions.why: Hit the health endpoint and one real user journey. It catches the configuration and connectivity failures that no amount of pre-deploy testing can, because they only exist in the target environment.
questions.asked: Connects testing to deployment; the strong answer says what the smoke test would have caught that CI did not.

questions.q: What is the difference between a fake and a spy?
choices: A fake is a working lightweight implementation; a spy records calls for later assertions
A fake throws on every call to prove errors are handled; a spy returns fixed values
A fake is created by a mocking library; a spy is a real object the test cannot change
A fake is used for databases only; a spy is used for HTTP clients and message queues
questions.why: An in-memory repository backed by a Map is a fake: it really stores and returns data. A spy wraps or replaces a function and remembers how it was called. Returning fixed values is a stub.
questions.asked: Vocabulary check before the "when do you use which" discussion.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a test data builder like `makeUser`?
choices: Tests run faster, because the default object is built once and then cached
Every test gets unique data, so tests can never interfere with each other
Each test states only the fields it cares about, and new fields are added once
Invalid users cannot be created, because it validates against the schema
questions.why: The test for admins says `role: 'admin'` and nothing else, so the reader sees what matters. When the model gains a required field, one builder changes instead of fifty literals. It builds a fresh object on every call and validates nothing.
questions.asked: A signal that you have maintained a large test suite, not just written a few tests.

questions.q: Using boundary value analysis, which ages should the tests for `canVote` include?
questions.code: const canVote = (age) => age >= 18;
choices: 0, 50 and 120, spread evenly across the realistic range of ages
17 and 18, the values on either side of the boundary in the rule
One random age on every run, so the whole range is covered over time
18 and 21, the ages at which voting rules change in most countries
questions.why: Off-by-one bugs live at edges: `>` instead of `>=` passes for 50 and fails only at 18. Testing 17 and 18 pins the exact boundary. Random ages would find it rarely, and not reproducibly.
questions.asked: A classic test-design question; it checks whether you choose inputs deliberately.

questions.q: `getUser` has a bug: for unknown ids it resolves instead of rejecting. What does this node:test test report?
choices: It fails with an assertion error raised by `assert.match`
It passes, because no assertion runs when nothing is thrown
It fails, because the resolved value escapes the try block
It times out, because the catch block is never entered
questions.why: A resolved promise skips the catch, so the test finishes with no assertion and is green. Use `await assert.rejects(getUser(999), /not found/)`, which fails when the promise resolves. Error paths are where tests most often assert nothing.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can spot a test that cannot fail, which is common in real suites.

questions.q: A test that uses randomly generated data fails about once a week and never on re-run. What makes it debuggable?
choices: Replace the random data with one fixed value, and delete the test if it still fails
Retry the test up to three times in CI, so a weekly failure no longer blocks merges
Generate data from a seeded generator and log the seed, so a failure can be replayed
Increase the amount of random data per run, so the failure shows up every time
questions.why: With the seed in the failure output you can rerun exactly the input that broke it, then turn it into a fixed regression case. Retrying hides a real bug, and fixing the data throws away the coverage randomness was giving you.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat flaky tests as bugs to reproduce, not noise to retry.

questions.q: What is a consumer-driven contract test?
choices: An end-to-end test that deploys the consumer and provider together in one shared environment
A legal agreement on uptime between teams, checked by a monitor in production
A load test in which the consumer team sets the traffic the provider must handle
The consumer records the requests and responses it relies on; the provider's CI verifies them
questions.why: Each side tests alone against a shared contract (Pact is a well-known tool), so a provider change that breaks a consumer fails in the provider's pipeline before deploy. No shared end-to-end environment is needed, which is what makes it cheaper and faster than deploying both together.
questions.asked: Comes up once services are split between teams; the strong answer says which pipeline fails.

questions.q: What does mutation testing measure that line coverage does not?
choices: Whether tests fail when the code is deliberately altered, such as `>` turned into `>=`
How much memory the code allocates when the tests mutate shared objects between runs, in bytes
Whether the code still compiles after dependencies are upgraded to new versions
How often the test suite itself changes, as a signal of brittle tests
questions.why: A tool makes small changes (mutants) and reruns the suite; a mutant that survives shows code that runs under test but is not really checked. It is slow, so teams run it on critical modules rather than on every commit.
questions.asked: A depth question that follows "is 90% coverage good?"; it shows you know how to test the tests.

questions.q: The second test fails when the file runs, but passes when run on its own. Why?
choices: node:test runs tests in parallel, so both push to the array at the same moment
The tests share the module-level `cart`, so state from the first leaks into the second
`assert.equal` compares arrays by reference, so the length check reads a stale copy of it
The first test's assertion fails silently and leaves the runner in a broken state
questions.why: Tests in a file run in order by default and share module state, so 'starts empty' sees the apple. Create fresh state inside each test or in `beforeEach`. A test that passes only in a certain order is a flaky test waiting for a reordering.
questions.asked: Order dependence is the commonest cause of flaky suites; spotting it in five lines is the junior bar.

questions.q: `getUser(1)` returns a new object `{ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }`. Why does this Vitest assertion fail?
questions.code: expect(getUser(1)).toBe({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' });
choices: `toBe` compares object keys in order, and `getUser` adds `name` first
`toBe` checks identity with `Object.is`, and these are two separate objects
`toBe` only accepts primitives and throws a type error for object arguments
`toBe` compares JSON strings, and the literal has a different key spacing
questions.why: `toBe` is `Object.is`: same primitive value or the very same reference. Two objects built separately are never the same reference, so use `toEqual` for value comparison. `toBe` accepts objects happily; it just compares identity.
questions.asked: The first matcher mistake everyone makes; a strong answer names `Object.is` and reaches for `toEqual`.

questions.q: What happens with this Vitest assertion, and which matcher would catch the difference?
questions.code: expect({ id: 1, deletedAt: undefined }).toEqual({ id: 1 });
choices: It fails; `toEqual` treats a missing key and an `undefined` key as different
It fails; use `toMatchObject` instead, which ignores keys that are undefined
It passes; `toStrictEqual` would fail it, since it checks undefined keys too
It passes; no built-in matcher distinguishes the two, so compare `Object.keys`
questions.why: `toEqual` recursively ignores properties whose value is `undefined`, so the two objects count as equal. `toStrictEqual` also checks undefined properties, array sparseness and class types, which matters when an API response must not carry a stray key.
questions.asked: Shows you know matchers have different equality rules, which matters when asserting API payloads.

questions.q: What does the last line log?
choices: [1, undefined, 9]
questions.why: Once-values are consumed first, in order; when they run out the default from `mockReturnValue` applies. The chain order does not matter: a later `mockReturnValue` does not override queued once-values.
questions.asked: Checks you can script a stub for a retry path: fail once, then succeed.

questions.q: The `vi.mock` call sits after the import of `signup`, which imports `./mailer.js`. Does `signup` get the fake mailer?
choices: No; the import ran first, so `signup` holds the real `send` binding
Only if `signup.js` is imported again with `await import()` in the test
No; `vi.mock` affects only the test file's own imports, not nested ones
Yes; Vitest hoists `vi.mock` above the imports before the file runs
questions.why: Vitest rewrites the file so every `vi.mock` call runs before any import, and the mock applies to the whole module graph, including `signup.js`'s own import. That hoisting is also why a mock factory cannot use variables declared lower in the file.
questions.asked: Module mocking looks like magic until you know about hoisting; interviewers probe whether you do.

questions.q: `parse('')` throws `Error('empty input')`. What does this test report?
choices: It passes, since `toThrow` sees that the call to `parse` threw an error
It fails with `empty input`, thrown before `expect` ever receives a value
It passes only if `parse` is async, because `toThrow` awaits the result
It fails with a message saying that `toThrow` needs a string argument
questions.why: JavaScript evaluates the argument first, so `parse('')` throws while building the call to `expect` and the test fails with that error. `toThrow` needs a function it can call itself: `expect(() => parse('')).toThrow()`. For async code use `await expect(p).rejects.toThrow()`.
questions.asked: A small trap that reveals whether you understand what an assertion actually receives.

questions.q: In Vitest, the spy is installed but the assertion fails with 10. Why?
choices: `price` calls its local `rate` binding, not the export the spy replaced
`vi.spyOn` needs `mockImplementation`, since `mockReturnValue` is for `vi.fn`
The spy only applies after `await`, because ES module exports load lazily
`mockReturnValue(2)` affects the second call only, and `price` calls it once
questions.why: Inside an ES module a call to `rate()` goes straight to the local function, whatever happens to the module's export object. Spying on the namespace only changes calls made through it. Fix the design: pass the rate in, or move `rate` to another module and mock that.
questions.asked: Separates people who mock by trial and error from those who understand module bindings, and usually leads to 'inject it instead'.

questions.q: On a spy created with `vi.spyOn(mailer, 'send').mockResolvedValue('ok')`, what is the difference between `mockClear()` and `mockRestore()`?
choices: `mockClear` deletes the fake result; `mockRestore` also wipes the call history
`mockClear` removes the spy; `mockRestore` keeps it but forgets its calls
`mockClear` wipes recorded calls; `mockRestore` puts the real `send` back
`mockClear` resets every spy in the file; `mockRestore` resets only this one
questions.why: Clear forgets `mock.calls` and `mock.results` but keeps the fake implementation, which is what you want between tests sharing a stub. Restore undoes the spying, so `mailer.send` is the original method again. Reset sits between them, dropping the fake implementation.
questions.asked: Knowing the clear/reset/restore ladder is how you avoid mocks leaking between tests.

questions.q: Test A calls `vi.spyOn(flags, 'isEnabled').mockReturnValue(true)`. Test B, later in the same file, expects the real flag value and fails only when A runs first. What is the fix?
choices: Move test B above test A, so the spy is not installed yet when B runs
Restore spies after each test, via `restoreMocks: true` or an `afterEach`
Run the file with `--sequence.shuffle` so the order changes each time
Mark test B with `test.concurrent` so it runs in its own module copy
questions.why: A spy replaces the method on a shared object until something restores it, so it leaks into every later test in that file. Restoring after each test removes the order dependency. Reordering hides it, and shuffling only exposes it more often.
questions.asked: Order-dependent failures are a classic; the strong answer fixes cleanup rather than order.

questions.q: Why use `vi.useFakeTimers()` to test a warning that appears 30 seconds before a session expires?
choices: The test can move time forward instantly and exactly, instead of waiting 30 s
Real timers are disabled in the test environment, so `setTimeout` never fires
Fake timers also stub `fetch`, so the session refresh never reaches the server
It makes `setTimeout` run synchronously, so the warning shows on the first line
questions.why: With fake timers, `vi.advanceTimersByTime(30_000)` fires due callbacks immediately and deterministically, so the test takes milliseconds and cannot race the clock. Timers still only fire when you advance them; nothing becomes synchronous by itself, and the network is untouched.
questions.asked: Tests that sleep are slow and flaky; interviewers want to hear that you control time instead.

questions.q: `isOverdue(invoice)` compares the due date with `new Date()`. Which Vitest setup makes the test deterministic without changing the function?
choices: `vi.spyOn(Date, 'now').mockReturnValue(Date.UTC(2026, 2, 1))`
`process.env.TZ = 'UTC'` at the top of the test file, before any import
`vi.useFakeTimers()` then `vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-03-01T12:00:00Z'))`
`vi.stubGlobal('Date', { now: () => Date.UTC(2026, 2, 1) })` in `beforeEach`
questions.why: `setSystemTime` fakes the clock that both `Date.now()` and a bare `new Date()` read. Spying on `Date.now` does not affect `new Date()`, which reads the clock directly, and stubbing `Date` with a plain object breaks the constructor. Fixing the time zone makes output stable but not the date.
questions.asked: Date-dependent tests are the top cause of 'fails on the 1st of the month'; a strong answer also mentions injecting a clock.

questions.q: How many tests does this report?
choices: One test, which contains three assertions run one after the other
Nine tests, one for each number that appears in the table of cases
Three tests, but the first failing row stops the remaining rows
Three tests, each named from its row, for example `add(2, -2) is 0`
questions.why: `test.each` generates one independent test per row, formatting the name with printf-style placeholders, so a failure names the exact case and the other rows still run. That is the point over a loop of assertions inside one test.
questions.asked: Table-driven tests are the idiomatic way to cover boundaries; interviewers like hearing that failures name the case.

questions.q: `createUser` returns an object with a random UUID `id`, the given `email` and a `createdAt` Date. Which assertion checks it without pinning the random values?
choices: `expect(user).toEqual({ id: expect.any(String), email, createdAt: expect.any(Date) })`
`expect(user).toMatchObject({ email })`, then `expect(user.id).toBeTruthy()` for the rest
`expect(JSON.stringify(user)).toContain(email)`, so extra fields cannot break it
`expect(Object.keys(user)).toEqual(['id', 'email', 'createdAt'])`, checking only keys
questions.why: Asymmetric matchers such as `expect.any(Date)` let the full shape be checked while tolerating values that differ each run. `toMatchObject` alone ignores extra or missing fields you care about, and the string or key-only checks miss wrong types.
questions.asked: Tests on generated ids and timestamps are everywhere in CRUD code; this shows you can keep them exact yet stable.

questions.q: A developer commits a stray `test.only`. What happens when Vitest runs in CI, where the `CI` environment variable is set?
choices: Only that test runs, and the pipeline goes green without the others
Vitest ignores `.only` in CI and runs the whole suite as normal
The run fails with an 'unexpected .only modifier' error instead
Vitest runs that test twice, once on its own and once with the suite
questions.why: Vitest's `allowOnly` defaults to false when `CI` is set, so a stray `.only` fails the run rather than silently skipping everything else. Locally `.only` works as a focus tool. Many teams also add a lint rule such as `no-only-tests`.
questions.asked: A realistic accident; the strong answer knows the tooling guard and mentions linting for it.

questions.q: Why prefer `vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_EXPORT', 'on')` to assigning `process.env.FEATURE_EXPORT = 'on'` in a test?
choices: Direct assignment is ignored, because `process.env` is frozen in test runs
`vi.stubEnv` encrypts the value, so it does not appear in the CI logs
`vi.stubEnv` also rewrites the `.env` file, so the app picks up the change
Vitest can undo stubbed values with `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` after each test
questions.why: A plain assignment persists for the rest of the worker, so later tests silently see the flag on. Stubbed values are tracked and restored, manually or with the `unstubEnvs` config option. Nothing touches files on disk.
questions.asked: Shows you think about cleanup and cross-test leakage, not just making one test pass.

questions.q: What does this mock give the tests in the file?
choices: A module whose only export is `today`, so other imports are undefined
The real module, with only `today` swapped for the fixed-date version
The real module, with `today` patched only in tests that call `vi.mocked`
A copy of the module that is reloaded for each test in the file
questions.why: A mock factory's return value becomes the entire module, so spreading the original keeps every real export and overrides just `today`. Without the spread, anything else imported from `dates.js` would be missing. The mock applies to the whole file, not per test.
questions.asked: Partial mocks are common in real suites; interviewers check you know a factory replaces the whole module.

questions.q: A query-string parser returns `'1'` where the test expects the number `1`. With the legacy `node:assert` import rather than `node:assert/strict`, what does `assert.equal(1, '1')` do?
choices: Throws, because the two values have different types
Passes, because legacy `equal` compares with `==`
Throws a deprecation error, since `equal` was removed
Passes only if both are converted with `String()` first
questions.why: Legacy assertion mode uses loose equality, so `1 == '1'` passes and `deepEqual` is equally forgiving. Import `node:assert/strict` (or use `strictEqual` and `deepStrictEqual`) so a number-versus-string bug from JSON or a query string is caught.
questions.asked: A quick check that you would catch type bugs in tests rather than hide them.

questions.q: In Node 24's test runner, what does this test log?
choices: 1, then 1
0, then 0
0, then 1
1, then 2
questions.why: Mocked timers fire only when time is advanced past their due point: 999 ms is not enough and one more millisecond is. Nothing fires on its own, and because it was a `setTimeout`, not `setInterval`, the callback runs once.
questions.asked: Shows you can test timeouts and retries with the built-in runner, without extra dependencies.

questions.q: What does this assertion check?
choices: That the most recent call to `send` had exactly these two arguments
That `send` was called once, with arguments matching these two exactly
That at least one call to `send` had matching arguments, in that order
That `send` was called with these arguments before any other mock ran
questions.why: `toHaveBeenCalledWith` passes if any recorded call matches, and `stringContaining` accepts any body containing 'Welcome'. To pin the count, add `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)`; for the latest call use `toHaveBeenLastCalledWith`.
questions.asked: Interaction assertions are easy to over- or under-specify; this checks you know exactly what one proves.

questions.q: The service calls `repo.findById(id).then(...)`. Which stub for `findById` makes it receive `user`?
choices: `vi.fn().mockReturnValue(user)`
`vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(user)`
`vi.fn().mockImplementation(user)`
`vi.fn().mockReturnThis(user)`
questions.why: `mockResolvedValue(user)` returns `Promise.resolve(user)`, so `.then` works like the real async repository. Returning the plain object makes `.then` undefined and the code throws; `mockImplementation` expects a function, not a value.
questions.asked: A basic async stubbing check; mismatched sync and async doubles cause confusing failures.

questions.q: Why pass property matchers to this snapshot?
choices: They mark `id` and `createdAt` as the only fields worth saving in the snapshot
They stop the snapshot being written until both fields hold real values
They make Vitest regenerate the snapshot whenever those two fields change
Those fields differ every run, so they are checked by type, the rest by value
questions.why: Without matchers the snapshot would record one run's UUID and timestamp and fail on the next. Property matchers assert the type and store a placeholder, while every other field is still compared exactly.
questions.asked: Snapshot tests that fail on every run get deleted; this shows you know how to keep them stable.

questions.q: Vitest runs each test file in an isolated module environment by default. What does that protect you from?
choices: Module-level state leaking between files; tests in one file still share it
Any shared state between tests, so no cleanup code is needed anywhere
Rows that one test file writes to a shared database being seen by another
Tests in the same file running at the same time and racing each other
questions.why: Isolation gives each file fresh module instances, so a module-level cache or mock in one file cannot leak into another. Within a file, tests share those modules, and external state such as a database, files or ports is not isolated at all.
questions.asked: Knowing what the runner isolates, and what it cannot, is what lets you reason about order-dependent failures.

questions.q: What is wrong with this test?
choices: `forEach` runs the callbacks in parallel, so the saves overwrite each other
`expect` cannot be used inside a callback, so the assertions are ignored
The test must be marked `async`, or `await` inside the callback is a syntax error
`forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the test ends before the assertions
questions.why: The test function returns synchronously, so the runner records a pass while the saves are still pending; failures surface later as stray unhandled errors, if at all. Use `for (const row of rows) { await ... }` or `await Promise.all(rows.map(...))` in an async test.
questions.asked: A green test that asserts nothing is worse than no test; interviewers want you to spot the unawaited work.

questions.q: Each test needs a fresh, empty in-memory repository. Where should it be created?
choices: In `beforeAll`, so it is built once and shared by the tests in the file
In `beforeEach`, so every test starts from its own new instance
At the top of the file, so it is ready before the first test is collected
In `afterEach`, so it is rebuilt after one test ends and ready for the next
questions.why: `beforeEach` runs before every test, so none can see another's writes and the order no longer matters. `beforeAll` or module scope share one instance across tests, which is how order-dependent failures start. Reserve `beforeAll` for expensive, read-only setup.
questions.asked: A junior check that you think about test independence from the first line of setup.

questions.q: What does the string argument to `toThrow` check here?
questions.code: expect(() => parse('')).toThrow('empty');
choices: That the thrown error's class is named `empty`
That the error's message is exactly `empty`
That the thrown error's `code` property is `empty`
That the error's message contains `empty`
questions.why: A string argument matches a substring of the message; a regex matches by pattern and an error class checks `instanceof`. For an exact message use a regex anchored with `^` and `$`, or assert on the caught error directly.
questions.asked: Asserting on the right error, not just any error, is what stops tests passing for the wrong reason.

questions.q: This file fails with "Cannot access 'fake' before initialization". Why, and what is the usual fix?
choices: `vi.fn` needs a type argument; add one, or declare `fake` with `let`
`vi.mock` is hoisted above `fake`; create `fake` inside `vi.hoisted()`
The factory must be async; return `Promise.resolve({ today: fake })`
The import must come after `vi.mock`; move the import line to the end
questions.why: Vitest lifts `vi.mock` to the top of the file, so its factory runs before `const fake` is initialised. `const { fake } = vi.hoisted(() => ({ fake: vi.fn() }))` is lifted too, so the factory can use it and the test can still assert on it. Moving the import changes nothing, since hoisting already reorders it.
questions.asked: A real error message from real suites; knowing why it happens shows you understand how module mocking works.

questions.q: In watch mode, you save a change to `src/pricing.js`. Which tests does Vitest re-run?
choices: Every test file in the project, in the same order as the last run
Only the test file with the same name, `pricing.test.js`, if one exists
The test files whose import graph includes `pricing.js`
Only the tests that failed on the previous run, until they pass
questions.why: Vitest tracks each test file's module graph and re-runs the files that import the changed module, directly or indirectly, which keeps feedback fast. Name matching would miss integration tests that reach `pricing.js` through another module.
questions.asked: An easy check of whether you use a fast feedback loop day to day.

questions.q: `new InvoiceService(repo, logger)` needs a logger, but the behaviour under test never logs. What kind of test double do you pass for `logger`?
choices: A mock, so the test can verify the logger was never called
A fake that writes to a temporary file the test deletes later
A dummy: any object that satisfies the parameter and is unused
A spy, so the test output shows everything that would have been logged
questions.why: A dummy only fills a slot; nothing reads from it or asserts on it. Using a mock here would add an assertion the test does not care about, which is exactly how tests become brittle.
questions.asked: Checks you use the lightest double that does the job rather than mocking everything.

questions.q: What is the defining difference between a mockist (London-school) unit test and a classicist (Detroit-school) one?
choices: Mockists write tests after the code; classicists always write the test first
Mockists replace every collaborator; classicists use real ones where cheap
Mockists test through the UI; classicists test functions one at a time
Mockists use a mocking library; classicists hand-write every test double
questions.why: Mockists isolate the class under test from all collaborators and verify interactions; classicists treat a 'unit' as a behaviour, use real in-process objects, and double only awkward things such as I/O. Both can do TDD; the split is about what gets replaced.
questions.asked: Opens a discussion about brittleness; naming both schools and their trade-off signals real experience.

questions.q: A 'sociable' unit test of `CheckoutService` does what?
choices: Runs against the shared staging database so the whole team sees its data
Is written by pairing, so two developers agree on every assertion in it
Replaces every class `CheckoutService` uses with a mock, even pure ones
Uses the real in-process collaborators, such as the price calculator
questions.why: Sociable tests let the unit talk to its real, fast collaborators and double only slow or non-deterministic edges such as the database or email. They survive internal refactors better than solitary tests that mock every class.
questions.asked: Shows you can talk about unit size precisely instead of equating 'unit' with 'one class'.

questions.q: Your code calls the Stripe SDK directly in several services, and every test mocks the SDK's methods. What does 'don't mock what you don't own' suggest instead?
choices: Call Stripe's live API from every test, so the tests are always realistic
Wrap Stripe in your own `PaymentGateway`, fake that, and test the wrapper
Record Stripe's HTTP responses once and replay them in each unit test
Mock only Stripe's HTTP client, so the SDK's own code still runs in tests
questions.why: A thin adapter you own gives services a small interface that is easy to fake, while the adapter itself gets a few integration tests against Stripe's test mode. Mocking the vendor's API spreads your guesses about it through every test.
questions.asked: A mid-level design question; the adapter-plus-integration-test answer is what interviewers want.

questions.q: `placeOrder` saves through a repository. Which assertion survives a refactor from `repo.save(order)` to `repo.saveMany([order])`?
choices: `expect(repo.save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ total: 30 }))`
`expect(repo.save).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)`, then checking the first argument
`expect(await fakeRepo.findAll()).toEqual([expect.objectContaining({ total: 30 })])`
`expect(repo.save.mock.calls[0][0].total).toBe(30)`, reading the call directly
questions.why: Checking the resulting state in an in-memory fake asserts the outcome, not the call used to reach it, so internal changes do not break it. The other three pin the exact method, which is an implementation detail here.
questions.asked: State versus interaction verification is a core design question; a good answer says when each fits.

questions.q: A module has a complicated private helper `normaliseAddress` that is not exported. How should it be tested?
choices: Export it with an underscore prefix so tests can call it but callers know not to
Use a test-only build that exposes private functions through a debug global
Leave it untested, since private code is covered by code review instead
Through the public function that uses it, or move it to its own module
questions.why: Tests through the public API survive refactoring of internals. If the helper is complex enough to need its own tests, it is a real unit: give it a module and a public API of its own. Exporting it for tests couples the tests to internals.
questions.asked: A common junior question; the strong answer treats 'I want to test this private' as a design signal.

questions.q: `applyLoyaltyDiscount` loads the customer, reads today's date, calculates the discount and saves the order. Which refactor makes the rule testable without any mocks?
choices: Extract a pure `discountFor(customer, order, today)` and keep the I/O in a thin shell
Make the function async throughout, so a test can await each step in turn
Split it into four exported functions and mock three of them in each test
Add optional parameters that let tests turn off loading and saving entirely
questions.why: Functional core, imperative shell: the decision becomes a pure function you test with plain values, and the shell that loads and saves is covered by a few integration tests. Test-only flags leave production code carrying paths that exist just for tests.
questions.asked: This is the design move behind most testable code; interviewers like to see you reach for it unprompted.

questions.q: `createInviteCode()` uses `crypto.randomUUID()` internally, and a test needs to assert the exact code stored. What is the cleanest approach?
choices: Assert only that the stored code has the length of a UUID and move on
Seed `crypto` with a fixed value in `beforeEach` so UUIDs repeat each run
Run the test several times and assert that at least one code matches
Inject an id generator, so the test passes one returning a known value
questions.why: Randomness is an input, like time: pass in `generateId` (defaulting to `crypto.randomUUID`) and the test controls it. Node's `crypto` has no seed you can set, and a length check would pass even if the wrong code were stored.
questions.asked: Checks that you treat non-determinism as a dependency, not something to work around in assertions.

questions.q: What does the humble object pattern recommend for an Express route handler that parses the request, applies business rules and writes to the database?
choices: Keep the handler thin and move the rules into a unit that has no HTTP types
Mock `req` and `res` fully, so the handler can be unit tested as written
Mark the handler as humble, which tells the coverage tool to ignore it
Split the handler into middleware functions, one for each business rule
questions.why: The hard-to-test boundary (HTTP, UI, the framework) is left so simple it needs little testing, while the logic moves somewhere it can be tested with plain values. Hand-built `req`/`res` mocks are brittle and still leave the logic tangled with transport.
questions.asked: Shows you know how to restructure framework-bound code for testing rather than fighting the framework.

questions.q: An API client's tests replace global `fetch` with `vi.fn()` and assert on its arguments. What usually goes wrong over time?
choices: `vi.fn()` cannot return a `Response`, so the client reads an empty body
Stubbing a global leaks into other files, since Vitest shares the global scope
The tests pin the exact call shape, so passing a `Request` object breaks them
Node 24's `fetch` is read-only, so the stub is ignored and the real call is made
questions.why: A function-level stub couples tests to how `fetch` is called (URL string or `Request`, header casing, option names), so behaviour-preserving refactors fail. Intercepting at the network layer, with MSW or undici's `MockAgent`, asserts on the HTTP request instead.
questions.asked: Discriminates people who have maintained mocked suites from those who have only written them.

questions.q: Why do Express apps often export the `app` from one module and call `app.listen()` in another?
choices: Express requires `listen` to run in a separate file when using ES modules
Tests can import the app and drive it with supertest without binding a port
It lets the app start faster, because all routes load before the server does
It stops the port number leaking into the bundle that ships to the browser
questions.why: supertest accepts an app and starts it on an ephemeral port per request, so tests never clash over a fixed port or leave a server running. The entry file stays the only place that listens in production.
questions.asked: A basic structure question for Node API testing; it shows you have actually wired tests to an app.

questions.q: Each integration test runs inside a database transaction that is rolled back afterwards. When does this isolation technique break down?
choices: When a test reads rows, because reads inside a transaction see no data
When the database is Postgres, which does not allow rollbacks in tests
When tests run one at a time, since rollbacks need parallel connections
When the code commits its own transaction or uses another connection
questions.why: Rollback isolation only works if every query goes through the test's connection and transaction. Code that opens its own transaction, uses a pool, or hands work to a queue worker escapes it, and its writes persist. Truncating tables or a fresh database per worker avoids that.
questions.asked: Interviewers probe whether you know the limits of the technique, not just its name.

questions.q: How should the test database get its schema before an integration suite runs?
choices: Run the same migrations that production runs, from an empty database
Copy the production database each night and run the tests against it
Have the ORM generate tables from the current models on every run
Keep a hand-written `schema.sql` for tests, updated when tests fail
questions.why: Applying the real migrations tests them too, so a broken migration fails CI instead of the deploy. Generating from models skips the migrations entirely, and copying production data brings personal data into test environments.
questions.asked: Links testing to deployment safety; a strong answer mentions that migrations are code that needs testing.

questions.q: Vitest runs test files in parallel workers against one Postgres server. How do you stop files clobbering each other's rows?
choices: Set `retry: 3` so a clobbered test passes on a later attempt
Give each worker its own database or schema, keyed by worker id
Wrap every query in `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` while tests run
Truncate every table in the `afterAll` hook of each test file
questions.why: Each worker gets an id (`VITEST_POOL_ID`), so setup can create `app_test_1`, `app_test_2` and so on, and files never share rows. Truncating after a file still races with other workers mid-run, and retries only hide the collisions.
questions.asked: A realistic scaling problem for test suites; the answer shows you understand where parallelism collides.

questions.q: An integration test posts an invalid body to `POST /orders` and asserts a 400 with a field error. Which extra assertion adds the most value?
choices: That the response time was under 200 ms, to catch slow validation
That the response has a `Content-Length` header matching its body
That no order row was written, so validation runs before the insert
That the error message text matches a snapshot of the whole response
questions.why: A 400 that still inserted a half-valid row is a real bug the status code hides; checking the database proves the side effect did not happen. Timing and full-body snapshots make the test brittle without covering a likely failure.
questions.asked: Tests that check side effects, not just responses, are what separate thorough from superficial API tests.

questions.q: Which set of tests gives the most confidence that only an order's owner can `DELETE /orders/:id`?
choices: Owner gets 204, and a request with a malformed id gets 400
Owner gets 204, run once each for an admin and a normal user
Anonymous gets 401, and the route is listed in the auth config
Owner gets 204, another user is refused, anonymous gets 401
questions.why: The dangerous bug is another signed-in user deleting someone else's order (broken object-level authorisation), so a test with a second real user is essential. Checking config or only the happy path would miss it.
questions.asked: Authorisation bugs are the top API vulnerability; interviewers like candidates who test the negative cases.

questions.q: What is the 'mystery guest' test smell?
choices: A test depends on data set up somewhere it does not show, such as a shared seed file
A test was written by someone no longer on the team, so nobody knows why it exists
A test calls a function whose name does not match what the test title describes
A test uses a random user from a pool, so a different guest appears on each run
questions.why: When the key fact (this user is an admin, this order is paid) lives in a distant fixture, a reader cannot see why the test should pass, and editing the seed breaks unrelated tests. Builders that state the relevant fields inline fix it.
questions.asked: Naming test smells precisely is a sign you have reviewed and maintained real suites.

questions.q: Why do many teams prefer DAMP (descriptive and meaningful phrases) over strict DRY in test code?
choices: Test code is not shipped, so duplication in it has no cost to anyone
Each test should read on its own, even if that repeats a little setup
Test runners cannot import shared helpers, so repeated code is required
DRY test helpers run slower, because each call adds a stack frame
questions.why: A failing test is read in isolation, often by someone else; if understanding it needs a tour of helpers and loops, it is slow to diagnose. Share builders and setup that hide noise, but keep the inputs and expectations that matter visible in the test.
questions.asked: Shows you have an opinion on test readability grounded in who reads failures.

questions.q: What is the problem with this test?
choices: It re-implements the rule in its branches, and a failure does not name the case
It runs too slowly, because loops inside a test are not optimised by the runner
`expect` cannot be called more than once per test, so only one branch is checked
It is fine, since looping over a sample list covers more cases than a table would
questions.why: Logic in a test duplicates the logic under test, so a shared misunderstanding (is 100 discounted?) passes both. Explicit rows with expected values, via `test.each`, state the rule plainly and report which input failed.
questions.asked: Conditional logic in tests is a classic review comment; interviewers check you can explain why.

questions.q: What does the guideline 'one assertion per test' really mean in practice?
choices: A test may call `expect` only once, so each field needs its own test
Each test should check one behaviour, even with several expectations
Every test should assert one value and use snapshots for everything else
A test file should contain one test per function in the module it tests
questions.why: The point is a single reason to fail. Checking status, body and the saved row of one request is one behaviour, while testing create and delete in one test is two. Splitting every `expect` into its own test multiplies setup for no gain.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you apply rules dogmatically or understand the reason.

questions.q: You must refactor a 400-line legacy pricing function that has no tests and no clear spec. What do you write first?
choices: Unit tests for the new functions you plan to extract from it
An end-to-end test clicking through checkout for one product
Characterisation tests that record what it currently returns
Nothing yet; refactor carefully, then add tests for the result
questions.why: Characterisation (golden master) tests capture current behaviour for a wide spread of inputs, bugs included, so the refactor can be checked for unintended changes. Fix bugs deliberately afterwards, with their own tests.
questions.asked: Legacy code is most of real work; this checks you have a safe way into it.

questions.q: Your OpenAPI spec says `GET /orders/:id` returns `total` as a number. What cheap test catches the implementation drifting from the spec?
choices: A snapshot of the spec file, so any edit to it fails the build
A unit test that constructs the response object by hand
A linter rule that checks every route has a spec entry
Validating real responses against the spec in API tests
questions.why: Running each integration-test response through a validator built from the spec turns the spec into an assertion, so a string `total` or a missing field fails CI. A snapshot or route lint only checks the documents, not what the API actually returns.
questions.asked: Shows you treat an API spec as a testable contract, which matters when other teams consume it.

questions.q: A payment webhook handler must be idempotent. Which test proves it?
choices: Send an event with a bad signature and assert the handler returns 400
Deliver the same event twice and assert the order is marked paid once
Send two different events at once and assert both responses are 200
Deliver one event and assert the handler responds within five seconds
questions.why: Providers retry deliveries, so duplicates are normal; the test replays the same event id and checks there is exactly one side effect (one payment row, one email). The signature and timing tests are useful but prove something else.
questions.asked: Idempotency comes up with any integration; a strong candidate knows how to test it, not just define it.

questions.q: Two customers try to buy the last ticket at the same moment. How do you test that only one succeeds?
choices: Send the two requests one after the other and assert the second gets 409
Mock the repository so the second call throws a conflict error
Fire both with `Promise.all` against a real database, expect one 409
Add a `setTimeout` in the handler during tests to widen the race window
questions.why: Only concurrent requests against the real database exercise the lock, constraint or conditional update that prevents overselling. Sequential requests pass even with a race, and a mock just asserts what you told it. Repeat the test a few times, since one run may not interleave.
questions.asked: Race conditions in CRUD apps are a favourite mid-level topic; testing them is the follow-up.

questions.q: Orders get `created_at DEFAULT now()` in Postgres. Why does `vi.setSystemTime` not make that value predictable in an integration test?
choices: `setSystemTime` fakes the clock in the Node process, not the database server's
Postgres caches `now()` per connection, so the first value is reused forever
Fake timers only affect `setTimeout`, and `Date` is not changed by them
Postgres rejects timestamps from clients whose clock is set in the future
questions.why: The default is evaluated by the database, which knows nothing about your test's fake clock. Either pass the timestamp from the application (via an injected clock) or assert a range around the real time.
questions.asked: Checks you know where fakes stop working, which is where confusing integration failures come from.

questions.q: What is a test fixture?
choices: A bug that has been fixed and now has a test to stop it coming back
The known state or data a test starts from, set up before it runs
A test that is pinned so it never runs in parallel with any other
The part of the CI configuration that decides which tests to run
questions.why: A fixture is the baseline a test relies on: seeded rows, a temp directory, a started server. Good fixtures are fresh for each test or read-only, so no test depends on another's leftovers. A fixed bug with a test is a regression test.
questions.asked: Vocabulary check that comes before questions about isolation and shared state.

questions.q: Why should unit tests not call a real third-party API such as a geocoding service?
choices: Third-party APIs block requests that come from Node's test runner
Real calls make tests slow, flaky, rate-limited and sometimes billed
Unit tests cannot use `await`, so real network calls never get to finish
The API's HTTPS certificate is not trusted inside test processes
questions.why: A unit test must be fast and deterministic; a network call brings latency, outages, quotas and cost into every run. Put the vendor behind an adapter you can fake, and cover the adapter with a few tagged integration tests.
questions.asked: An opener that leads to how you structure boundaries and what you test against the real service.

questions.q: In an integration test, the email service is replaced by an in-memory outbox that stores each message. What does that let the test do?
choices: Check that the real SMTP server accepts the message format used
Skip sending entirely, so no assertions about email are possible
Assert on the recipient and content of mail the app actually sent
Measure how long the email provider takes to deliver each message
questions.why: A fake with a working, inspectable implementation lets the test read `outbox[0].to` and the subject after the request completes, asserting on outcome rather than on method calls. Whether the real provider accepts the message is a separate adapter test.
questions.asked: Shows you prefer inspectable fakes at the boundary over brittle call-count mocks.

questions.q: What makes a test 'flaky'?
choices: It fails on every run until someone updates its expected values
It passes and fails on the same code, without any change to either
It takes longer than the runner's timeout on slower CI machines
It covers code that changes often, so it needs frequent manual edits
questions.why: Flakiness means the result is not a function of the code: timing, ordering, shared state, time zones or the network leak in. A test that fails every run is simply failing, and one that needs edits is brittle, which is a different problem.
questions.asked: The definition matters because the fix for flaky and brittle tests is different.

questions.q: This test passes on a developer laptop in London and fails on a teammate's laptop in New York. Why?
choices: `toLocaleDateString` ignores the locale argument unless the ICU data is installed
`en-GB` formatting is only available when the machine's own locale is British
A date-only string parses as UTC midnight, which is 28 February in New York
`new Date('2026-03-01')` is parsed as month-first, so it means 3 January
questions.why: ISO date-only strings are parsed as UTC, and formatting uses the machine's local zone, so west of Greenwich the date rolls back a day. Pin the zone in the formatter (`timeZone`) or in the test environment, and build dates with an explicit offset.
questions.asked: Time-zone bugs are the classic 'works on my machine' test; a good answer fixes the code, not just CI.

questions.q: An API test asserts `GET /users` returns `[ada, grace]` in that order. It passes for weeks, then fails after a database upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The query has no `ORDER BY`, so the row order was never guaranteed
The new database version sorts rows alphabetically by name by default
The upgrade changed the default JSON serialiser for arrays
The test database kept rows cached from before the upgrade
questions.why: Without `ORDER BY`, SQL databases return rows in whatever order is convenient, which can change with versions, plans, vacuuming or parallel scans. Add an explicit order if clients rely on it, or compare without order in the test if they do not.
questions.asked: Shows you know which ordering is a contract and which is an accident.

questions.q: A test starts a background export, then does `await sleep(200)` before asserting the file exists. It fails occasionally on CI. What is the best fix?
choices: Raise the sleep to 2000 ms, so slow CI machines always have enough time
Mark the test `retry: 3`, since timing issues pass on a second attempt
Move the test to a nightly job where the machines are less loaded
Await the export's own promise, or poll with a timeout until it exists
questions.why: A fixed sleep is a guess about how long work takes: too short flakes, too long slows every run. Wait for the actual completion signal, or use a polling helper such as `vi.waitFor` or `expect.poll` that returns as soon as the condition holds.
questions.asked: Sleeps in tests are a top flakiness cause; interviewers want 'wait on a condition'.

questions.q: Your team turns on automatic retries for failed tests in CI. What else should it do so retries do not hide bugs?
choices: Retry only on the main branch, so pull requests still fail on the first error
Report which tests passed only after a retry, and fix or quarantine them
Raise the retry count until the flaky rate on the dashboard reaches zero
Retry each whole CI job instead, so every test gets a fresh machine
questions.why: A retry turns a flaky failure green, and some flakes are real race conditions in the product. Tracking 'passed on retry' keeps them visible so each gets an owner. More retries only make the signal quieter.
questions.asked: Checks you treat retries as a tourniquet, not a cure.

questions.q: What does quarantining a flaky test usually mean?
choices: Deleting it and opening a ticket to rewrite it from scratch later
Running it only on the developer's machine who last touched it
Running it in a non-blocking job, with an owner and a deadline to fix
Marking it `skip` until the flaky behaviour stops happening by itself
questions.why: Quarantine keeps the test running and visible without blocking merges, while the ticket and deadline stop it becoming permanent. Skipping or deleting loses the coverage and the signal about how often it fails.
questions.asked: Shows you can keep a pipeline trustworthy without throwing tests away.

questions.q: Several test files each start the API on port 3000. Run in parallel, some fail with `EADDRINUSE`. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Listen on port 0 so the OS assigns a free port, and read it back
Add a short random delay before each file starts its server
Close every server in a global `afterAll` hook that runs last
Pick a random port between 3000 and 4000 inside each test file
questions.why: Port 0 asks the operating system for any free port; `server.address().port` gives the one assigned, so collisions cannot happen. Random ports and delays make clashes rarer, not impossible. supertest already does this when you pass it the app.
questions.asked: A practical parallel-testing problem with a crisp answer; interviewers like the port-0 trick.

questions.q: Why turn on test order shuffling (for example Vitest's `sequence.shuffle`) in CI?
choices: It spreads slow tests evenly across workers, so runs finish sooner
It exposes tests that only pass because an earlier test set things up
It prevents the runner caching results between two runs of the suite
It makes each test run twice, once in each order, to find any flakiness
questions.why: A test that silently relies on another's leftovers passes in the usual order and fails when shuffled, revealing the hidden dependency. Log the seed so a failing order can be replayed. It does nothing for speed.
questions.asked: Shows you think about isolation proactively rather than debugging order issues when they bite.

questions.q: A test for `renewalDate` (today plus one month) has passed for months, then fails on 31 January. What is the right response?
choices: Skip the test on the last day of each month, when the date maths is unreliable
Treat it as flaky, since passing on other days proves the function correct
Change the assertion to allow any date within three days of the expected one
Fix the date in the test and add 31 January as a case: it found a real bug
questions.why: `setMonth` overflows: 31 January plus one month is 3 March in 2026. The test was right to fail; its problem was depending on today's date, which is why it only showed up once a month. Freeze the clock and cover month ends explicitly.
questions.asked: Separates 'flaky' from 'found a real edge case', which interviewers care about.

questions.q: Tests only ever pass `isMember: false` to this function. What does a coverage report show?
choices: Full line coverage, but branch coverage below 100%
Lines one and two uncovered, since `isMember` is false
Full line and branch coverage, since every line ran
Branch coverage at 100%, but line coverage at 67%
questions.why: Every line executes, so line coverage is complete, but the `isMember ? 0` branch never ran. Branch coverage counts each side of every condition, which is why it is the more useful number for logic-heavy code.
questions.asked: Checks you know which coverage number to look at and what each can hide.

questions.q: What is a sensible way to use a coverage threshold in CI?
choices: Require 100% so that every line in the codebase is guaranteed tested
Set it just below the current level so coverage cannot quietly drop
Require 80% on each file, including configuration and generated code
Avoid thresholds, since any coverage number encourages gaming it
questions.why: A floor near today's level stops untested code sneaking in while avoiding pressure to write assertion-free tests to hit a target. Use the report itself to find risky untested areas; 100% mandates tend to produce tests that execute code without checking it.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a pragmatic view of coverage, not a number.

questions.q: In TDD's refactor step, what must stay true?
choices: Coverage must rise, since refactoring adds new branches to test
At least one test must be failing, to guide the next change
The tests stay green: structure changes, behaviour does not
The public API is renamed to match the new internal structure
questions.why: Red, green, refactor: refactoring means changing structure with behaviour held fixed, and the passing tests are the proof. If a test goes red during refactoring, you changed behaviour or the test was coupled to implementation.
questions.asked: A simple check of whether you have actually done TDD or only read about it.

questions.q: Your first TDD test is `expect(vat(100)).toBe(20)`, and `return 20` makes it pass. What does triangulation suggest next?
choices: Delete the hard-coded value and write the full implementation straight away
Add a second example, such as `vat(50)` being 10, to force the general rule
Assert on the function's source code, to ensure it is not hard-coded
Replace the test with a snapshot, which will catch any hard-coded value
questions.why: Triangulation adds examples until the only simple implementation is the real one. A second input breaks the constant and drives out `amount * 0.2`. It keeps each step small and gives the rule more than one witness.
questions.asked: Shows real TDD practice rather than just the slogan.

questions.q: Which bug does `tsc --strict` catch with no tests written at all?
choices: A discount rule that applies at 100 when the spec says above 100
A query that returns orders in the wrong order for the account page
Passing a possibly `undefined` user to a function that needs a `User`
An API call that sends the wrong customer id to the payment provider
questions.why: Strict null checks make 'maybe undefined' part of the type, so the call fails to compile. The other three are logic errors where the types are all correct, which is what tests are for. Types and tests catch different classes of bug.
questions.asked: Opens a conversation about how types and tests complement each other.

questions.q: Which typescript-eslint rule reports `saveOrder(order);` where `saveOrder` returns a promise that nobody awaits or handles?
choices: `no-unused-vars`
`require-await`
`no-floating-promises`
`no-unused-expressions`
questions.why: `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` uses type information to find promises that are neither awaited, returned nor given a `.catch`, which is how rejected saves disappear silently. `require-await` flags async functions without `await`, a different problem.
questions.asked: A lint rule that prevents a whole class of production bugs; naming it shows hands-on experience.

questions.q: A pull request fixes a bug and adds a test. How can a reviewer check that the test really covers the fix?
choices: Check that coverage for the changed file went up in the CI report
Run the new test twice and check that it passes both times
Check that the test's name mentions the ticket number for the bug
Revert the fix locally, run the test and check that it fails
questions.why: A regression test that passes without the fix proves nothing. Seeing it red without the change and green with it is the only real evidence. Rising coverage just shows lines ran, not that the behaviour was asserted.
questions.asked: Shows you review tests with the same scepticism as production code.

questions.q: What is a regression test?
choices: A test that checks performance has not become slower than the last release
A test that pins a fixed bug or existing behaviour so it cannot return unseen
A test that runs the previous release alongside the new one to compare output
A test that is run only before a release, rather than on every single change
questions.why: Regression tests guard behaviour that already works, typically written when a bug is fixed, so the same bug cannot come back silently. Any test in a suite that runs on every change acts as regression protection.
questions.asked: Vocabulary check that leads into 'how do you handle a production bug'.

questions.q: What does a canary release catch that a thorough pre-production test suite cannot?
choices: Syntax errors in the code, before any user downloads the new build
Type errors in the new code, since canaries run the TypeScript compiler
Failing unit tests, which are re-run on a small set of real servers
Problems that only appear with real traffic, data and infrastructure
questions.why: Sending a small share of production traffic to the new version, while watching error rates and latency, surfaces issues no test environment reproduces: real data shapes, load, and third-party quirks. Rollback limits the blast radius.
questions.asked: Shows you see testing as continuing after deploy, with observability as the test oracle.

questions.q: A new checkout flow ships behind a feature flag. How should tests handle the flag?
choices: Cover both flag states while it exists, then delete the old path's tests
Test only the flag-on path, since that is the one that is going to ship soon
Test only the flag-off path, since that is what users see in production
Mock the flag service to return random values so both paths get covered
questions.why: While the flag exists both paths are live code that can break; once it is removed, the dead branch and its tests go too. Random flag values make results depend on luck, which is a flakiness recipe.
questions.asked: Feature flags are common in real teams; interviewers check you have thought about their testing cost.

questions.q: What is the main cost of relying on end-to-end tests for most of your coverage?
choices: They cannot run in CI, because they need a real browser and a real person
They cannot test the database, because they only see the rendered page
They are slow and flakier, and a failure rarely says which part broke
They require every developer to learn a separate programming language
questions.why: An end-to-end failure could be the UI, API, database, network or test itself, so diagnosis is slow, and each test takes seconds. Keep them for a few critical journeys and push detail down to faster tests. They do run headless in CI.
questions.asked: Checks you can explain the trade-off behind the shape of your suite.

questions.q: A Vitest suite takes 18 minutes in CI. What does `vitest run --shard=1/3` on three parallel jobs do?
choices: Runs the slowest third of the test files first on each of the three jobs
Splits the test files into three groups and runs one group on each job
Runs each file three times across the jobs to detect flaky failures
Runs only a third of the suite on each push, rotating through all three
questions.why: Sharding partitions the files, so three machines run the whole suite once in about a third of the time; merge the reports afterwards. Nothing is skipped, which is what separates it from sampling.
questions.asked: Pipeline speed is a real team concern; knowing sharding shows you have worked on one.

questions.q: A pipeline runs only tests affected by changed files (for example `vitest --changed origin/main`). What is the risk?
choices: It runs every test anyway, because Git reports all files as changed in CI
It cannot see TypeScript files, so changes to `.ts` sources are missed
It re-runs tests that already passed, which makes the pipeline slower
Changes outside the import graph, such as config or SQL, can be missed
questions.why: Affected-test selection follows imports. A changed environment file, migration, JSON fixture read at runtime or a dependency bump may alter behaviour without appearing in any import chain, so run the full suite on main or before release.
questions.asked: Shows you know the limits of speed optimisations in a pipeline.

questions.q: What does a static analysis tool such as CodeQL add beyond a project's unit tests?
choices: It runs the unit tests faster by caching their results between commits
It traces data flow to find risky patterns such as SQL built from input
It proves the code is free of bugs, so fewer tests need to be written
It generates unit tests automatically for every single function it can read
questions.why: Static analysis reasons about all paths without running them, spotting tainted input reaching a query or a shell even where no test goes. It raises candidates, with false positives, and proves nothing about correct behaviour, which is still the tests' job.
questions.asked: Checks you know which tool catches which class of problem.

questions.q: What property does this fast-check test assert?
choices: That `encode` never returns the same output for two different strings
That `encode` and `decode` are both fast enough for any string length
That decoding an encoded string gives back the original, for any input
That `decode` throws for any strings that were not produced by `encode`
questions.why: This is a round-trip property: fast-check generates many strings, including empty, Unicode and odd whitespace, and checks each survives the trip. It finds edge cases a handful of hand-picked examples miss.
questions.asked: Round-trip is the most useful property in CRUD code (serialisers, parsers, URL encoding), so it is a good first example.

questions.q: A fast-check property fails. Why is the counterexample it reports usually tiny, such as `" "`?
choices: fast-check only generates short strings, so failures are always small
The runner truncates long values to keep the failure message readable
It shrinks the failing input to a minimal case that still fails
It reports the first input generated, which is usually the smallest
questions.why: After a failure, property-based libraries shrink: they try smaller variants of the input and keep any that still fail, ending with a minimal counterexample. It also prints a seed so the run can be replayed exactly.
