questions.asked: Knowing about shrinking shows you have actually debugged a property-based failure.

questions.q: An integration test that seeds a database needs 12 seconds and hits Vitest's per-test timeout. What is the best first step?
choices: Raise `testTimeout` for the whole project to 60 seconds so nothing times out
Find out why it is slow, then raise the timeout for that test or file only
Move the test to `beforeAll`, where the runner does not enforce timeouts
Split the test into four parts that each finish just under the limit
questions.why: A 12-second test usually means seeding far more than needed or a missing index. Fix that first, and if it is still legitimately slow, give that test or file a longer timeout so fast unit tests still fail quickly when they hang.
questions.asked: Checks you treat slow tests as a signal rather than turning the dials globally.

questions.q: Tests marked `test.concurrent` in one file each stub global `fetch` with different responses. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing; concurrent tests each run in their own worker with their own globals
Vitest rejects `vi.stubGlobal` inside concurrent tests with a clear error
The stubs are applied in alphabetical order of the test names in the file
They share one global, so a test can see another's stub mid-run
questions.why: Concurrent tests in a file run interleaved in the same module scope, so global stubs and module state collide and results depend on timing. Keep tests that touch globals sequential, or inject the dependency per test.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what 'concurrent' shares before reaching for it to speed things up.

questions.q: What is a `describe` block for in Vitest or Node's test runner?
choices: Grouping related tests under one name, with hooks that apply to that group
Running the tests inside it in parallel with every other test in the file
Documenting a test without running it, like a comment that shows in reports
Marking tests that describe expected behaviour, as opposed to bug fixes
questions.why: `describe` nests tests so the report reads as a hierarchy (`OrderService > cancel > refunds a paid order`) and scopes `beforeEach` and friends to that group. It does not change how or when the tests run.
questions.asked: Basic structure; follow-ups usually ask how hooks nest.

questions.q: What is the difference between `test.skip('refunds partial orders', ...)` and `test.todo('refunds partial orders')`?
choices: `skip` runs the test but ignores its result; `todo` never runs anything
`skip` is reported only locally; `todo` fails the run when `CI` is set
`skip` disables a written test; `todo` records a test not written yet
`skip` hides the test from reports; `todo` shows it as a failed test
questions.why: Both appear in the report without running. `todo` takes just a name and marks planned work; `skip` switches off an existing test body, and a skipped test left for months is dead coverage worth a lint warning.
questions.asked: Small, but it shows whether you leave visible markers for missing tests instead of silently deleting them.

questions.q: `findUser(id)` returns `null` when nobody matches. Which assertion is the most precise for that case?
choices: `expect(result).toBeFalsy()`
`expect(result).toBeNull()`
`expect(result).toBeUndefined()`
`expect(result).not.toBeTruthy()`
questions.why: `toBeNull` passes only for `null`. `toBeFalsy` and `not.toBeTruthy` also pass for `undefined`, `0` or an empty string, so they would hide a bug that returns the wrong empty value; `toBeUndefined` fails outright.
questions.asked: Precise assertions catch more bugs; this is a quick check that you pick them deliberately.

questions.q: Why does `expect(users).toContain({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' })` fail even though `users` holds an object with those exact fields?
choices: `toContain` works only on strings, so an array argument always fails
`toContain` checks identity; `toContainEqual` compares objects by value
`toContain` needs the object's keys in the same order as in the array
`toContain` looks only at the first element unless you pass it an index
questions.why: `toContain` uses `===`, so it finds primitives or the same object reference. For a value match inside an array use `toContainEqual`, or `expect.arrayContaining` with `expect.objectContaining` when only some fields matter.
questions.asked: A daily matcher mix-up; knowing the pair shows fluency with the tool.

questions.q: What does `npm test` run in a Node project?
choices: Every file ending in `.test.js`, using npm's own built-in test runner
The command in the `test` script of `package.json`
Vitest, which npm downloads if the project does not have it installed
The tests of every dependency listed in `node_modules`
questions.why: npm has no test runner of its own; `npm test` is shorthand for `npm run test`, which runs whatever the `test` script says, such as `vitest run` or `node --test`. That script is what CI calls.
questions.asked: A basic check that you know how a project's test command is wired up.

questions.q: How does a CI job know that the test suite failed?
choices: It searches the log output for the word FAIL printed by the runner
The runner uploads a report file, and CI reads the failure count
The runner exits with a non-zero status code, which fails the step
It compares the number of tests with the count from the last run
questions.why: Every CI system treats a command's exit code as success (0) or failure (anything else). Test runners exit non-zero on any failed test or error, so wrapping them in a script that swallows the exit code silently makes CI green.
questions.asked: Shows you understand the plumbing, which matters when a pipeline is green but should not be.

questions.q: What is the difference between a test runner and an assertion library?
choices: The runner writes the tests; the assertion library runs them in CI
The runner is for unit tests; the assertion library is for end-to-end
The runner is only used locally; the assertion library is used in CI
The runner finds and runs tests and reports; assertions check values
questions.why: The runner (Vitest, Node's `node --test`, Jest) discovers files, runs tests and hooks, isolates them and reports. The assertion library (`expect`, `node:assert`, Chai) throws when a value is wrong. Vitest and Jest bundle both.
questions.asked: Vocabulary that shows you understand the pieces of a test stack.

questions.q: What is equivalence partitioning?
choices: Grouping inputs that should behave the same and testing one from each
Splitting the test suite into equal parts so each CI job runs the same time
Checking that two implementations return equal results for all inputs
Writing one test for each equality operator the function uses internally
questions.why: For a quantity field, 'valid 1 to 99', 'zero or negative', 'too large' and 'not a number' are partitions; one test per partition covers the behaviour without testing every value. Pair it with boundary values at each edge.
questions.asked: Test-design vocabulary that shows you choose cases methodically rather than at random.

questions.q: A junior's PR adds `POST /projects`, with one test showing a valid body returns 201. Which tests are most often missing?
choices: A performance test proving the endpoint stays under 100 ms at peak
Failure cases: invalid body, unauthenticated, forbidden and conflict
A snapshot of the full JSON response, to catch any unexpected field
A test that the route is listed in the README's table of endpoints
questions.why: Most production bugs and security holes live on unhappy paths: missing validation, missing auth checks, duplicate handling. The happy path is the one a developer checks by hand anyway.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for candidates who test failure behaviour by default.

questions.q: What is a false positive in testing?
choices: A test that reports failure although the code works correctly
A test that passes, and the code really does work as intended
A test that is skipped but still counted as passed in the report
A test that passes, though the code it covers is actually broken
questions.why: Following the usual convention, a positive is a reported failure: a false positive is a failing test with nothing wrong, like a flaky or brittle one. A green test over broken code is a false negative, and that is the dangerous kind, since nobody investigates it.
questions.asked: Both failure modes of a suite matter; strong answers explain which one erodes trust and which one ships bugs.

questions.q: What does test isolation mean?
choices: Each test runs in its own Docker container with its own database
Each test lives in its own file, with nothing shared between files
Each test can run alone or in any order and gets the same result
Each test mocks every dependency, so it touches no other module
questions.why: Isolation is about outcome: no test depends on another's leftovers or order. You get it with fresh setup per test, cleanup, and unique data; containers and mocks are possible tools, not the definition.
questions.asked: Foundation for every flakiness question; interviewers expect the behavioural definition.

questions.q: A snapshot test fails after you intentionally changed the output format. What is the correct next step?
choices: Delete the snapshot file, so a fresh one is written on the next run
Mark the snapshot test as skipped until the output has settled down
Review the diff, and if every change is intended, update with `-u`
Run the suite again, since snapshots often fail on the first run
questions.why: The snapshot diff is the review: confirm each change is the one you meant, then accept it with `vitest -u` (or `u` in watch mode) and commit the updated file. Blindly updating turns snapshots into tests that always pass.
questions.asked: Checks that you treat snapshot updates as a reviewed change rather than a chore.

questions.q: What does `vi.fn()` give you with no arguments?
choices: A function that throws until an implementation has been provided
A function that returns `undefined` and records every call made
A copy of the most recently imported function, with calls recorded
A function that returns a resolved promise with `undefined` in it
questions.why: A bare `vi.fn()` accepts any arguments, returns `undefined`, and records `mock.calls` and `mock.results`. You then shape it with `mockReturnValue`, `mockResolvedValue` or `mockImplementation`. It is sync unless you make it async.
questions.asked: Baseline mocking fluency before harder questions about mock lifecycles.

questions.q: What is exploratory testing good for, next to an automated suite?
choices: Replacing unit tests on code that changes too often to automate
Proving the release is bug-free before it goes to production
Finding problems nobody thought to write an automated test for
Measuring the code coverage that the automated tests miss
questions.why: Automated tests only check what someone anticipated. A person deliberately poking at a feature (odd inputs, double-clicks, back buttons, slow networks) finds the unanticipated, and each find can become an automated test.
questions.asked: Shows you do not think automation is the whole of quality.

questions.q: Why run an Express API's tests with Vitest's `environment: 'node'` rather than `'jsdom'`?
choices: jsdom cannot run `async` functions, so every one of the API tests would time out
jsdom adds browser globals and set-up cost that server code should not have
The `node` environment mocks the network, so no real requests are made
The `node` environment is required before supertest can be imported
questions.why: Server code should run where it will run in production. jsdom injects `window` and `document`, which can mask code that wrongly depends on them and slows start-up. `node` is Vitest's default for good reason.
questions.asked: Checks you configure the test environment to match production.

questions.q: Why should a unit test suite run in seconds, not minutes?
choices: CI providers charge per test, so fewer seconds means fewer tests billed
Slow suites are skipped by the runner once they exceed a time budget
Developers run fast tests constantly, so mistakes are caught in minutes
Test runners cache results only for suites that finish in under a minute
questions.why: Feedback speed decides how often tests get run: a suite that takes seconds runs on every save, while a slow one runs only in CI, long after the context is gone. Speed is why the bulk of logic tests avoid real I/O.
questions.asked: An opener about why the shape of a suite matters to daily work.

questions.q: Your team's integration tests call a shared staging API that other teams also deploy to. Why is that suite not hermetic, and why does it matter?
choices: Its result depends on services and data it does not control, so it flakes
It uses HTTPS, which makes requests non-deterministic across different runs
It runs in CI, and hermetic tests are ones that only run on a laptop
It has more than one assertion per test, which hermetic tests forbid
questions.why: A hermetic test brings up or fakes everything it needs, so only your change can alter its outcome. Depending on a shared environment means another team's deploy or data clean-up can fail your build. Use containers or fakes, and keep a few separate smoke tests against shared environments.
questions.asked: Shows you know why 'it failed because staging was down' is a design problem.

questions.q: Tests share a database without truncating between files, and `users.email` is unique. How do you keep creates from colliding?
choices: Catch unique-violation errors in the tests and treat them as a pass
Drop the unique constraint in the test database's migrations
Give each test unique data, such as an email with a random suffix
Run the files in alphabetical order so emails are created once
questions.why: Unique per-test data (`ada+${randomUUID()}@test.dev`) lets tests coexist and run in parallel; assertions then look up their own rows rather than counting the whole table. Changing the schema for tests means you are no longer testing the real one.
questions.asked: A practical isolation technique; interviewers like candidates who do not weaken the schema for tests.

questions.q: Why does this assertion pass, and which matcher would fail it?
questions.code:
class Money { constructor(amount) { this.amount = amount; } }

expect(new Money(5)).toEqual({ amount: 5 });
choices: `toEqual` ignores the class; `toStrictEqual` checks the type too
`toEqual` calls `valueOf`; `toBe` would compare the two prototypes
`toEqual` compares JSON strings; `toMatchObject` checks classes
`toEqual` checks the class first; no matcher would fail it here
questions.why: `toEqual` compares own enumerable properties recursively and ignores the prototype, so a `Money` equals a literal with the same fields. `toStrictEqual` also checks the type, which matters when behaviour lives on the class.
questions.asked: Shows you know exactly what 'equal' means to your assertion library.

questions.q: A helper retries a failing call with `await sleep(1000 * 2 ** attempt)`. With fake timers, why does `vi.advanceTimersByTime(3000)` leave it stuck after the first attempt?
choices: Fake timers do not support exponential values larger than 1000 ms
Each sleep starts after a promise settles, and the sync call never flushes it
`vi.advanceTimersByTime` only advances `setInterval`, not `setTimeout`
The retry helper must be mocked with `vi.fn()` before timers affect it
questions.why: The first rejection is handled in a microtask, so the first sleep's timer does not exist yet when the synchronous advance runs. `await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(3000)` interleaves promise flushing with timer firing, letting each retry schedule its next sleep.
questions.asked: Testing retries is common and this trap is real; knowing the async variant signals hands-on experience.

questions.q: Stryker reports a surviving mutant that changes `total >= 100` to `total > 100` in the free-shipping rule. What does that tell you?
choices: The mutation tool found a bug, so `>=` should become `>` in the code
The rule is too complex and should be split into two separate checks
The tests are flaky, since the mutant passed some runs and failed others
No test checks a total of exactly 100, so the boundary is unprotected
questions.why: A survivor means the suite passes whether the boundary is inclusive or not, so nobody would notice if it changed. Add a test at exactly 100 (and 99.99) that pins the intended rule. The mutant is not a proposed fix.
questions.asked: Reading mutation results well shows you understand what tests are for, not just that the tool exists.

questions.q: All tests pass, yet Vitest reports an 'Unhandled Rejection' error and exits non-zero. Why is failing the run the right behaviour?
choices: Unhandled rejections crash Node 24, so the run is incomplete anyway
A rejection that escaped a test usually means an assertion ran unseen
Vitest treats all of the console output from tests as an error in CI mode
The error is always caused by the runner itself, not the tested code
questions.why: A rejection outside any awaited chain often comes from a floating promise in a test or the code: an assertion that ran after its test finished, or an error the app swallows. Failing the run keeps that from hiding behind a green report.
questions.asked: Checks you investigate stray errors rather than muting them.

questions.q: A Vitest `globalSetup` file starts a Postgres container and wants tests to know its connection string. How does it pass the value?
choices: Assign it to a module-level variable that the test files import
Attach it to `globalThis`, which the worker processes all share
Write it into `vitest.config.ts`, which reloads after global setup
Call `provide('dbUrl', url)` there, and `inject('dbUrl')` in tests
questions.why: `globalSetup` runs once in the main process, while tests run in separate workers, so its variables and globals are invisible to them. `provide`/`inject` (or an environment variable set before workers start) carries serialisable values across.
questions.asked: Shows you understand the process model behind a test runner, which explains many 'why is this undefined' puzzles.

questions.q: In a Pact contract between a web app and an orders API, what is a 'provider state' such as `order 42 exists`?
choices: A health check the provider must pass before the consumer runs its tests
A version tag that states which provider release the contract applies to
A setup hook the provider runs to create that data before replaying
A cached response the consumer uses when the provider is unavailable
questions.why: Each recorded interaction assumes some data exists. When the provider verifies the contract, it calls a state handler to seed `order 42` before replaying the request, so verification does not depend on whatever is in a shared database.
questions.asked: Follows up 'what is contract testing' to see whether you have actually run one.

questions.q: `POST /orders` saves the order and queues a 'send confirmation' job for a worker. How should an integration test assert the email?
choices: Sleep for a few seconds after the request, then check the outbox
Assert only the 201, since background work cannot be tested
Run the queued jobs in-process, then assert on the fake outbox
Mock the queue so the job function is never called in tests
questions.why: Draining the queue deterministically (an in-memory queue, or calling the worker's handler on each queued job) tests the whole flow without waiting on real time. Sleeping is flaky, and mocking the queue away leaves the job itself untested.
questions.asked: Background work is where test suites get flaky; interviewers want a deterministic strategy.

questions.q: A migration splits `users.name` into `first_name` and `last_name`, backfilling existing rows. What should its test check?
choices: That the migration file name follows the team's usual timestamp convention
That the down migration deletes both new columns without an error
That the migration finishes within the deployment's time budget
That representative existing rows are backfilled into the right parts
questions.why: The risky part is the data transformation: single names, extra spaces, compound surnames. Seed realistic rows, run the migration, and assert the results. Timing and rollbacks matter too, but they are not where data gets silently mangled.
questions.asked: Data migrations are the change most likely to hurt production; testing them shows maturity.

questions.q: Vitest's coverage report lists `src/utils/date.js` at 100% even though you know `formatRange` has a bug. How is that possible?
choices: Coverage only reports files changed in the current branch
Every line ran, but no assertion checked `formatRange`'s result
The coverage tool skips functions that contain string templates
Coverage at 100% means the bug must be in another file instead
questions.why: Coverage records execution, not verification: a test that calls a function and asserts nothing, or asserts on something else, still marks every line green. That is why coverage is a map of untested code, not proof of tested code.
questions.asked: Checks you can explain what coverage cannot tell you, with a concrete example.

questions.q: A test double for `PaymentGateway` returns `{ status: 'ok' }`, but the real gateway returns `{ status: 'succeeded' }`. What would have caught this?
choices: Raising the unit test coverage threshold for the checkout module
Running the unit tests with `--sequence.shuffle` to vary their order
Typing the fake against the same interface the real adapter uses
Adding more mocks so every code path sees the `ok` status too
questions.why: If the fake and the real adapter both implement one TypeScript interface with `status: 'succeeded' | 'failed'`, the fake cannot return `ok`. A small adapter test against the provider's sandbox keeps that interface honest.
questions.asked: Drifting fakes are the main weakness of test doubles; typing them is a cheap defence.

questions.q: What is the point of a code review checklist item such as 'does every new branch have a test'?
choices: It replaces the need for any coverage tools in the CI pipeline
It makes missing tests a normal thing to ask for, not personal
It lets reviewers approve without reading the code itself
It guarantees the change has no bugs once every box is ticked
questions.why: Shared expectations make 'where is the test for the error case?' a routine question rather than a criticism, and catch gaps tools cannot judge, such as whether the test asserts the right thing. A checklist supplements reading the code; it does not replace it.
questions.asked: Shows you think about team habits around quality, not only individual skill.

questions.q: What is the main job of a test's failure message?
choices: To tell the reader what broke and why, without opening the test file
To print a stack trace of the runner so that the CI logs can be searched
To store the failure in the snapshot file for the next test run
To notify the author of the test by email when it starts failing
questions.why: A good name plus a precise assertion ('expected status 403, received 200 for another user's order') lets whoever sees the red build diagnose it quickly. Vague checks such as `expect(ok).toBe(true)` throw that information away.
questions.asked: Checks you write tests for the person who will read the failure.

questions.q: A pure `calculateTax(order)` is unit tested with 40 cases. Checkout also has a test through the real API and database. What should that API test cover?
choices: All 40 tax cases again, to prove the maths works end to end
Nothing about tax, since the unit tests already cover it fully
Only the database schema, since HTTP is covered by the framework
One or two cases, to prove the tax is wired into the saved order
questions.why: Detail belongs in fast unit tests; the integration test proves the pieces are connected, for example that the saved order and response carry the computed tax. Repeating every case slows the suite and doubles the maintenance when rules change.
questions.asked: This is the testing-strategy question in miniature: what goes at which level, and why.
